structure.title: I. A Model of Household Listing Behavior

observations.statement: The paper states its estimand as structural preference parameters (reference dependence, loss aversion, financial-constraint penalty) recovered from a two-period search-and-bargaining model of the house-selling decision, rather than a reduced-form treatment effect.

The introduction explicitly names three confounds that could generate a spurious loss-aversion pattern in listing prices: down-payment financial constraints, unobserved-quality measurement error in fair value, and optimization frictions from concave buyer demand, and previews how the model separates them.

The reference point for loss aversion is assumed to equal the nominal original purchase price throughout, an assumption the authors call restrictive but defend using the sharp bunching of realized sales at exactly that point as nonparametric supporting evidence.
observations.locator: Section I.B footnote; Section III.C Fact 3

observations.statement: The design variant is named as a mixture model of precise versus imprecise price targeters, which nests linear reference dependence and reference dependence plus loss aversion as special cases so the paper can distinguish them using different data moments.

The model section closes with an explicit paragraph mapping each of the three core structural parameters to a distinct qualitative feature of the data (slope over gains, excess bunching at the reference point, slope over home equity), stating how each is separately identified ahead of estimation.
observations.locator: Section I, end of model discussion

observations.statement: Multiple administrative registers (tax and transaction records, the housing register, mortgage data from the central bank, civil registration data) plus a private listings vendor are merged at the property and household level, with each source's own coverage period stated separately before the merge.

The share of official sale transactions that could be matched to listings data is reported explicitly, and final sample counts are broken out separately for listings, unique households, unique properties, and the full property-year housing-stock panel used for the extensive-margin analysis.

Each sample exclusion (foreclosures, zero-size properties, extreme prices, within-family and flagged-anomalous transactions, non-owner-occupier buyers, summer houses, owners of more than three properties) is paired with a substantive justification in a footnote, mostly appeals to thin or non-market pricing.

The seller demographic, income and wealth data are drawn from population-wide official Danish civil and tax registers linked by personal and household identification numbers, a scope of administrative microdata access that is not further characterized as restricted or public within the read pages.

The full property-year housing-stock sample used for the extensive-margin (listing propensity) analysis is explicitly distinguished from the transaction-level listings sample used for intensive-margin analysis, filtered with the same criteria but retaining repeated observations per property across years.

Potential gains and potential home equity are constructed as log differences between the hedonic-model predicted fair value and, respectively, the nominal original purchase price and the outstanding mortgage balance, both expressed as percentages via the log approximation.

The listing premium is defined as the log difference between the observed initial listing price and the hedonic fair-value prediction; the realized premium and realized gain are analogous log differences computed from the eventual sale price rather than the list price.

Fair house value is estimated from a hedonic pricing regression of log sale price on time-varying property characteristics, year-by-municipality fixed effects, an apartment-versus-house indicator interacted with those characteristics, and a polynomial in the lagged tax-assessed valuation, then applied out of sample to unsold listings and the full stock.

The two demand primitives that convert a listing premium into a sale probability and a realized price premium are estimated directly from the data (using a bounded generalized logistic function for the concave sale-probability curve) and then treated as fixed, data-implied inputs to the structural model rather than free parameters.

The paper distinguishes two conceptually separate sources of measurement error in fair value, time-varying unobserved property quality and idiosyncratic over- or under-payment at purchase, and states that each is handled with a different corrective strategy in the estimation.

A dedicated table lays out every state variable, calibrated parameter and structural parameter with its economic meaning and whether it is observed, estimated or calibrated, functioning as a glossary presented before any results rather than a regression table.

The main structural-parameter table reports eight nested model variants as rows, each adding a friction or a set of moments relative to the previous row, with bootstrap standard errors in parentheses beneath each estimate and a companion panel of check marks indicating which frictions and moments are active in each variant.

Because estimation matches binned data moments rather than running a single regression, the paper frames its specification progression as a sequence of model variants, successively adding concave demand, imprecise targeting, down-payment constraints, the extensive margin, a preference notch, and cross-sectional moments.

The hedonic pricing specification's fixed effects (year interacted with municipality) are named explicitly in the equation and text rather than only in a table note, since the hedonic step is reported as a formula rather than a results table with output columns.

Standard errors for the structural parameters are computed by re-estimating the entire pipeline, hedonic model, demand functions, moments and structural parameters, on bootstrap resamples clustered at the shire level; the shire-level clustering choice is stated but not separately justified in the text read.

The hedonic pricing regression used to construct fair-value predictions is reported with a fit statistic but without any discussion of standard errors, clustering, or inference for its own coefficients, consistent with its role as a prediction step rather than a causal specification.

A footnote reports how the hedonic model's fit statistic changes when estimating in levels instead of logs, when dropping the tax-assessor valuation regressor, and under an out-of-sample split-sample check, as a diagnostic of the valuation model's stability rather than of the structural estimates themselves.

A footnote checks that property and household observables, including renovation expenditures, are balanced and smooth around the potential-gains and listing-premium thresholds, explicitly likening this check to the identifying-assumption diagnostics used in regression kink designs and citing that literature.

A companion regression kink design implementation of the listing-premium hockey stick is described as carried out in the online appendix, with an explicit caveat that the paper does not expect a sharp kink there given its own account of smoothing frictions in the main model.
observations.locator: Section III.E footnote; online Appendix I.6

observations.statement: Excess bunching mass at the reference point is quantified against an explicit counterfactual distribution built from potential (rather than realized) gains, with bootstrap-based confidence bands shown directly on the bunching figure, following the bunching-estimator literature.

An instrumental-variable check using housing-stock homogeneity as an instrument for demand concavity is reported to confirm that instrumented demand concavity predicts cross-regional variation in the listing-premium slope, but is described narratively in a footnote with the mechanics deferred to the online appendix rather than shown as a first-stage table.

Robustness of the bunching evidence to round-number effects, to subsamples split by property holding period, and to subsamples split by reference-price quintile is summarized narratively in the main text with pointers to the corresponding online appendix subsection rather than shown as a table.

A dedicated table re-estimates the complete structural parameter vector under three alternative hedonic fair-value models, adding renovation-expense controls and two repeat-sales specifications, plus an inverse-variance-weighted alternative to the baseline equal-weighting scheme, summarizing all variants in one panel.

A simulation exercise perturbs the model with seller-side private information about property quality that is invisible to the econometrician, reconstructs de-biased data moments under this alternative information structure, and checks that recovered structural parameters are not materially altered.

The paper decomposes the aggregate price-volume correlation into contributions from down-payment constraints, reference dependence and loss aversion by sequentially switching on each ingredient in the estimated model and recomputing the model-implied correlation, presented as a cumulative and marginal decomposition.

Regional variation in demand concavity is linked to the homogeneity of the local housing stock as an intermediate explanatory step, motivating why buyers penalize high listing premia more sharply in markets where comparable properties make quality easier to assess.

Interaction between financial constraints and behavioral responses is explored graphically and with a formal regression of listing premia on potential gains conditioning on home-equity bins (and the reverse), but the paper explicitly labels the resulting pattern as one its own model cannot rationalize and flags it as unexplained.

Reference dependence and loss aversion are interpreted in relative terms, as the share of utility that realized gains contribute relative to final price, and as the multiple by which losses weigh more heavily than equivalent gains, and are situated against the range of prior lab and field estimates.

The moving-shock and search-cost parameters are translated into externally interpretable units, an annualized share of hedonic house value discounted at an independently sourced long-term mortgage-bond return, so abstract utility parameters map onto a benchmark the authors call empirically realistic.

Overall structural fit is summarized with a single average prediction-error statistic across all matched moments, and the text explicitly names which pattern in the data the preferred model fails to match rather than reporting only where the fit succeeds.

The authors state plainly that their model cannot rationalize the finding that financially constrained sellers display weaker reference dependence and loss aversion, explicitly framing this as an open puzzle for future theoretical work rather than something the paper resolves.

The unconditional level of the annual listing propensity is explicitly described as beyond the scope of what the model can explain, since doing so would require taking a strong stance on the drivers of the underlying moving shock, which is instead treated as a normalized, partly calibrated device.

Findings are framed throughout in terms of the specific Danish mortgage-market rules, down-payment regulation and sample window, and one validation exercise explicitly ties the model to the observed trajectory of Danish aggregate prices and volumes over that particular window, without a claim that the magnitudes transfer elsewhere.

Figures throughout use binned-average plots with polynomial or nonparametric smoothers overlaid, and several explicitly report bootstrap-based confidence bands as dotted lines around the binned averages rather than relying on analytic standard errors.

The structural-parameter tables report standard errors in parentheses beneath each point estimate together with a check-mark panel showing which frictions and moments are active in each column, rather than using a conventional asterisk-based significance-stars convention.

The paper relies heavily on a large lettered online appendix, cited dozens of times throughout for additional figures, derivations, and alternative specifications, none of which is included in the text supplied for this reading.

The introduction previews the paper's main structural estimates and their qualitative interpretation, and explicitly previews the empirical pattern the model fails to explain, ahead of any formal results section.

The paper is organized model-first: the structural model is presented in Section I before the data and reduced-form facts in Sections II-III, and a roadmap paragraph at the end of the introduction lays out this section-by-section ordering explicitly.

Robustness and validation material is grouped into its own dedicated section placed after the main structural estimates, kept separate from the reduced-form robustness checks that appear earlier alongside the descriptive facts.

A front-matter footnote directs readers to the article's online DOI landing page for additional materials and author disclosure statements, and the reference list separately cites a formal AEA data-and-code repository record for the paper.
observations.quote: additional materials and author disclosure statements

observations.statement: The data section labels its main sources as government administrative registers, with a single private commercial listings vendor as the only non-government source, but defers the procedural details of obtaining data access to a numbered online appendix subsection rather than describing the approval process in the main text.
observations.locator: Section II; References entry for Statistics Denmark

concordance.paper_says: The paper's primary estimator for its main claims is a structural model fit by classical minimum distance, matching binned empirical moments to model-implied moments, not a single regression or RD design.
concordance.card_shows: The card records only two designs, an OLS hedonic regression (d1/s1) and a local-polynomial RD/kink (d2/s2); no structural or minimum-distance design is recorded anywhere in the card.
concordance.note: Card coverage is partial (8 of about 56 code files read); the structural estimation code (4_0_Analysis_Paper.do, 4_1_1_Settings.py, 4_1_5_Model.py) was read but not turned into a design/specification record.

concordance.paper_says: The hedonic fair-value model is estimated as an OLS regression of log sale price on hedonic characteristics and year-by-municipality fixed effects.
concordance.card_shows: Card specification s1 records the same command and formula, an OLS regression with the identical fixed-effects structure.

concordance.paper_says: The hedonic model's fixed effects are described as year-cross-municipality fixed effects, with the municipality count stated as ninety-eight geographic units.
concordance.card_shows: Card specification s1 lists fixed_effects as year and komstr, matching the year-by-municipality structure.

concordance.paper_says: The main text does not discuss standard errors or clustering for the hedonic pricing regression itself; it is used purely as a valuation/prediction step feeding into the structural moments, not for direct inference.
concordance.card_shows: Card specification s1 records se.type and se.cluster_level as null.

concordance.paper_says: The appendix regression-kink implementation of the listing-premium hockey stick is only briefly described in a main-text footnote, which states a caveat about the expected shape but does not give a bandwidth or polynomial order.
concordance.card_shows: Card specification s2 shows a formula with a local-polynomial order and derivative but no bandwidth value; s2.sample is null.

concordance.paper_says: The appendix regression-kink check is a single-threshold kink design at a zero potential-gains cutoff, with no separate treatment/comparison group beyond the two sides of the running variable.
concordance.card_shows: Card specification s2.comparison_group is null, consistent with a kink design having no distinct comparison-group field.

concordance.paper_says: The paper names four core administrative data sources plus one commercial listings vendor, each with its own stated coverage period, as the inputs to the merged analysis dataset.
concordance.card_shows: The card's top-level data array is empty; no data sources are recorded in the card at all.

concordance.paper_says: The hedonic model's control set is spelled out in the text: time-varying lot size, interior size, room and bathroom counts, a vacancy dummy, building age, rural and historic dummies, distance to the nearest city, each interacted with the apartment indicator, plus a polynomial in lagged tax valuation.
concordance.card_shows: Card specification s1.controls_summary is null; only the outcome variable and a macro placeholder for the control set appear in the single evidence snippet read.

concordance.paper_says: No mention of regression weights appears in the discussion of the hedonic pricing model or the appendix RD check in the pages read.
concordance.card_shows: Card specifications s1.weights and s2.weights are both null.

concordance.paper_says: The paper reports an extensive set of diagnostics: hedonic fit-statistic checks, balance and smoothness checks around thresholds, bunching excess-mass estimates with bootstrap standard errors, and a demand-concavity instrumental-variable check.
concordance.card_shows: The card's diagnostics array is empty.

concordance.paper_says: The paper reports a dedicated robustness table re-estimating the full structural parameter vector under alternative hedonic valuation models and an alternative moment-weighting scheme, plus narrative bunching robustness checks.
concordance.card_shows: The card's robustness array is empty.

concordance.paper_says: The paper contains four numbered main tables and ten main figures reporting structural estimates, moment fits, and diagnostics.
concordance.card_shows: The card's outputs.tables and outputs.figures arrays are both empty.

gaps: No explicit justification found in the main text for choosing the shire level (rather than municipality or another unit) for the bootstrap-clustered structural standard errors, beyond naming it as the resampling unit.
No preregistration, IRB approval, or ethics/consent statement found anywhere in the read pages.

No explicit statement in the main text of the software or optimization package used to solve and estimate the structural model (the recipe card shows Stata and Python source files, but the paper text itself does not name the software).

No formal first-stage or weak-instrument statistic reported in the main text for the demand-concavity instrumental variable check; it is described narratively and the mechanics are deferred to an online appendix section.

No description in the main text of the procedure for obtaining access to the restricted Danish administrative registers; the paper points to an online appendix subsection (C.6) for those details, which was not supplied for this reading.

The online appendix (referenced dozens of times, spanning lettered sections A through K) was not included in the supplied text, so appendix-only diagnostics, derivations and robustness detail are recorded here only as referenced by the main text, not verified directly.

reading.note: Read the full main text supplied (pages 1-43: title/abstract, introduction, model, data, reduced-form facts, structural estimation, validation, conclusion, references) via sequential chunked reads plus a targeted grep/sed pass to confirm no line ranges were skipped between chunks. The paper's online appendix (sections A-K, cited extensively throughout) is a separate document not included in harness_build/papers/text/aer_112_10_8.txt and was not read; all appendix-only content is recorded as referenced, tagged online_appendix_not_available where relevant.
